sections.title: 1. Performance: undo, and Hazel compiled to JS
sections.intro: Two threads from the last meeting. Undo: what it costs as programs grow, and how close it can get to O(log n). And a new experiment decided there: compile livelits' view functions to JavaScript, to see how much faster Hazel code can get. Measured in Node on #2635 (livelits × modular editors) unless an item says otherwise.

items.title: Toward 60 fps: hazel-jit so far, and try it
items.asked: Matthew, 2026-11-08 (the goal: a 60 fps floor for small edits)
items.status: a click on a Witch slider shows in the picture in 19 to 24 ms, and a drag runs at 57.6 to 58.6 fps; build 45 (11-10) takes a step's statics to 12 to 18 ms, from 19 to 53
items.body:
Where it stands: on the Witch slide, a step shows in 19 to 24 ms and a drag runs at about 60 frames a second (^report(51), the Hazel-JIT Status Report, for colleagues: twenty numbered builds of trial/694-view-jit, hazelgrove/hazel#2817, each measured in Firefox and named by every figure). A step took 4.17 to 6.52 s on build 1, nothing compiled in the run; 176 to 290 ms on build 8, the figures here (^report(50)); and 19 to 24 ms on build 12, which draws from the compiled run first and edits the program after the paint. A drag ran at 9.8 frames a second on build 5, 48.4 on build 8, 57.6 on build 12 (171 of its 173 frames within 16.7 ms) and 58.6 on build 15 (173 of 177).

What is left is the work after the paint. The edit of the program is still made after each step: 126 to 193 ms of statics, syntax, the view and the outline on build 20 (^ticket(721), a choice below). New, 11-10: build 45 patches the edited item's statics instead of analyzing it again: a step's statics take 12 to 18 ms, from 19 to 53 on build 43, and the edited item's part 3 to 6 ms, from 13 to 42 (one run each). It passed CI and is on the branch since 11-10, 12:46 (^report(52)). It is also the kind of special case Matthew Keenan warns about (below, in "Fewer, deeper fixes"); ^report(53) proposes keeping it as a measurement of what finer-grained statics would buy, and landing per-item statics on dev first. The worker runs the whole program again for the probes, and its answer comes 1.4 to 2.0 s after the step; the page then spends 80 to 193 ms on it. Builds 13 to 20 took the page's work after a step from 0.56 to 0.92 s down to 0.21 to 0.32 s: the outline out of the view, the livelits an edit does not touch kept, the autosave out of the update, the projectors an answer does not change kept, and the worker's answer 198 KB, from 590 (no final stream the page dropped, and its first-order values sent as data, ^ticket(718)).

Try it with the frame-rate overlay: the Witch, compiled (the branch's latest build); build 8, with every Livelit Playground slide linked, is hosted by hazelgrove/hazel#2819; the overlay alone for dev is hazelgrove/hazel#2818.
items.meeting: The edit after a step (^ticket(721)): build 45 shows a model-only patch saves 10 to 35 ms of statics a step. Keep it as that measurement and land per-item statics on dev first, as ^report(53) proposes, or take the patch further (syntax, outline) on the branch? Should the overlay go to dev now? Would the team try the build?

items.title: Why Hazel is slow: a thousand cuts
items.status: report 048: the 196 costs the series measured, from 33 reports, by the four design choices they come from
items.body: New, 11-08: Cyrus asked why Hazel is slow; Matthew says death by a thousand cuts, and ^report(48) is the substance behind it (report 048). The series has measured 196 separate costs in 33 reports; many are most of the workload they were found in, and many make one another larger, so removing the largest exposes the next. They come from four design choices, each applied everywhere: values held as terms (42 costs: ids on every node, environments substituted in, run-time type checks on values, probes writing values out); whole-program work on every edit (75); values moved as terms across boundaries (44); and an interpreter that pays for the editor at every step (27: per pass about 20 times a Fumola step). Most fixes are on the livelits and trial branches; of the PRs against dev the ledger names, two are merged and nine open. The Witch's small edit, change by change: 4.2 to 6.5 s, now 1.3 to 1.7 s, still 80 to 100 times a 60 fps floor. Matthew Keenan answered it on Slack on 11-09, the next item.
items.meeting: Which of the four families to change first? Is a 60 fps floor for small edits the right yardstick for Hazel?

items.title: Fewer, deeper fixes: Matthew Keenan's reply to report 048
items.asked: Matthew Keenan, on Slack, 2026-11-09; Matthew's replies 11-09 and 11-10
items.status: report 053: his message, Matthew's replies, and our response to each point; six fixes would address the causes of 116 of the 196 costs
items.body:
New, 11-10: Matthew Keenan's gut reaction to report 048 is to fix the costs together, in a few well-chosen changes, not one at a time; an agent fixing them one by one would spread special-case logic through the codebase. ^report(53) quotes his message and Matthew's replies, and answers each point from the series' numbers: they bear out each point the series measured, with two refinements (a hash belongs on the node it describes; a probe's environments are large only on their way to the page).

Six fixes, all from his message, would address the causes of 116 of the 196 costs: Merkle hashes in the grammar; cheap ids kept temporary inside the evaluator; a value's type checked once; the worker as a language server; per-item statics on dev; and Bonsai for derived state. Ids and per-item statics can start now; the others are design work first. The hazel-jit branch stays a prototype and a measurement; ^report(52) ranks its changes and orders a redo by hand. The report ends with the causes his message left out, the interpreter and the JS boundary the largest, each with a question for a gut opinion.
items.meeting: Do we agree on the six fixes, or a different short list, and in what order? Who takes ids and per-item statics, which can start now? A gut opinion on the interpreter and the JS boundary, the causes no fix here addresses.

items.title: Undo and redo in O(log n), in space and in time: how close are we, and why not yet?
items.status: measured; the O(log n) design is open
items.body:
Matthew showed Cyrus the analysis of undo's cost on 2026-11-05 (^report(38)). The two questions continue: how do we get closer to O(log n) for an undo and a redo, in space and in time, and why are we not there yet, in each.

Time, where it stands. Every step grows in proportion to the program: on a program of n top-level definitions, an edit, an undo and a redo each have a log-log slope of 1.1 to 1.16 (^report(36)). Three fixes on #2635 made each step cheaper without changing that: the program's root id read from a cache (394552d5d0), no completions after a numeral (bfa36a6ede), and realizing the view after an undo no longer counted as an edit (9df1b2601e). Now a redo costs about an edit (41 ms against 46 at 3,200 definitions, dev build, one run), and an undo costs an edit plus a rebuild of the outline (85 ms).

Time, why not O(log n) yet. The incremental caches do their part: an edit, an undo or a redo re-parses one or two definitions and re-measures one or two chunks. What is linear is a handful of passes around them that walk every top-level definition: MakeTerm's top-level pass (about 38% of the profile at 3,200 definitions), DefStatics' walk of the chain of definitions (20%), the outline rebuilt from scratch on an undo (15%; only #2469's modular editors have it) and Measured's walk (6%). None of it is the undo history: pushing and popping an entry costs almost nothing. The top level is a list of definitions, so any pass over it, or any summary of it rebuilt after a change, is O(n). Not measured yet: evaluation and the view during an undo.

Space, where it stands. Dev keeps a whole copy of the editor for every edit, and caps the history only when a setting that is off by default is on (on #2597, Full Body kept 89 MB more per edit). Andrew Blinn's compaction (6010128b7d, on #2469 and #2635) drops each entry's derived data and keeps its zippers: then an entry adds about 0.01 MB at 400, 1,600 and 6,400 definitions, flat, because consecutive entries share nearly all their structure (^ticket(665), GitHub run 41695584813).

Space, why not O(log n) yet. Two parts are still linear. The newest entry of each stack is kept whole so that the latest undo is fast (032fe3aca6): 0.55, 1.9 and 6.9 MB at the three sizes, about 1.1 KB a definition. And what compaction drops (syntax, statics, evaluation) is rebuilt on a restore, so the space saved is paid in time. One caveat on the flat number: the probe typed into the same definition again and again; edits spread over the program may share less.

Toward O(log n), the candidates. (a) The top level as a balanced tree of definitions, each node with summaries of its subtree (the names it binds, its part of the skeleton, its rows): each pass touches only the edited definition's path, an entry shares every other node, and the worker's request after an edit shrinks the same way (^ticket(666) found a one-literal edit re-sends about 10% of a chain of lets, every let around the edit hashing anew). (b) Undo as an inverse edit applied to the live state, so derived data updates as it does for a keystroke and no snapshot needs rebuilding. (c) First, and cheapest: build the outline incrementally, which every undo pays for, and every edit while the sidebar is shown.
items.meeting: Cyrus's read of the two directions, a balanced tree of definitions or undo as an inverse edit, and which to prototype first. Is the incremental outline the right first step? For space: does flat-per-compacted-entry answer the question, or should the next measurement spread edits over the program, use a release build, or count the newest whole entry differently?

items.title: hazel-jit: livelit views compiled to JS, to see the best case
items.status: compiled code runs 13 to 1,140 times faster than the interpreter; a livelit's definition compiles in about a millisecond, a slide's whole run in 87 to 299 ms, once; ^report(51) says how to use it in a PR
items.body:
hazel-jit compiles an elaborated Hazel term to the source of a JavaScript function, and the browser runs it: 13 to 1,140 times faster than the interpreter on the programs measured (^report(51), for colleagues and their agents: expected gains and costs, how to use it in a PR today, what was added since the first version, its limitations, and next steps). On trial/694-view-jit (hazelgrove/hazel#2817), each livelit's view is compiled, and so is a slide's whole run, with each livelit's model a parameter (^report(49)); where it meets a form it does not compile, that code runs on the interpreter instead.

The costs: a livelit's definition compiles in about a millisecond, the largest, a module of 62,077 nodes, in 14 to 21 ms; a slide's whole run, 24,000 to 112,000 nodes, in 87 to 299 ms (median 153), once, nearly all of it writing the JS; loading the slides with many livelits is no slower. The limits: JavaScript's numbers, no probes inside compiled code, the forms it does not compile (holes, tests, quotations and a few more), one browser measured, and not on dev.

For dev, the values it carries: ^report(47), a design note for ^ticket(718), proposes closed first-order values as a form of their own, with no ids, holes, closures or sharing, measured against Hazel's terms and Fumola's values; on the branch, sending the worker's sample values that way took its answer from 475 to 198 KB, and the page's decoding from 24 to 31 ms to 7 to 8. Its questions for Matthew are open.
items.meeting: Is the best-case framing right, numbers allowed to differ? Is hazel-jit ready for colleagues to try in their own PRs, and on which branch? Is first-order data as a form of its own (^report(47)) worth a plan for the group?

items.title: BuckleScript and ReScript (and Melange): to know, and to compare with
items.status: compared in report 046 on two programs: the Petri rule, and the Witch's picture view
items.body:
Update, 11-07 11:45: the second program, a view (report 046, a view). The Witch slide's ^picture view, written again in ReScript and OCaml and by hand, on the slide's own picture (133 shapes, 924 points): by hand 0.17 ms, Melange 0.17, ReScript 0.18, js_of_ocaml 0.19, hazel-jit 0.19 (about 5,200 to 6,000 fps), all drawing the same SVG, byte for byte. Most of the work is one builtin, 1,985 numbers formatted with toFixed (0.14 ms alone), so the compilers converge; js_of_ocaml through OCaml's Printf takes 1.0 ms. A table of what holds across both programs: the compilers differ in calls, matches and layouts, and converge where a builtin does the work. Each compiled view has a page of its own.

Update, 11-07: compared, in report 046 (^ticket(698)). Report 043's Petri rule, written in ReScript and in OCaml, compiled by ReScript 12.3.1, Melange 5.0.0 and js_of_ocaml 5.9.1, beside hazel-jit's output and a hand-written handler, each listing in the report. A call, in Node: Melange 0.46 µs, ReScript 0.55, js_of_ocaml 0.71, by hand 0.90, hazel-jit 1.59, the interpreter 358. ReScript's and Melange's code reads like the hand-written: a function's arguments as JS arguments, === on ints, loops for tail calls, options without a box, records as objects. Those are report 046's five suggestions for hazel-jit, and each section of its end weighs one route: hazel-jit as it is, ReScript or Melange as a back end, js_of_ocaml, by hand, the interpreter.

Cyrus named BuckleScript and ReScript as technologies to know about, and perhaps compare with, if not use. What they are, briefly, to be checked as part of ^ticket(698): BuckleScript, from Bloomberg (2016), compiled OCaml to readable JavaScript. Its team later renamed it ReScript, with a syntax of its own, aimed at the JavaScript world (version 12 in 2026). Melange is a fork that kept OCaml and Reason syntax, with first-class support in dune. Hazel itself is compiled to JS by js_of_ocaml, which works from OCaml's bytecode: a different route.

Three ways they bear on hazel-jit: (1) a reference for its output, since they map a typed functional language's values to JS (variants, records, lists, closures, functions of several arguments) and are known for fast, readable output; (2) a route to use: turn Hazel into OCaml, Reason or ReScript and let their compiler make the JS, ahead of time, or in the page if their compiler runs there; (3) Hazel's own build: what Melange's output would do to the speed of Hazel's evaluator, against js_of_ocaml's, a larger question.
items.meeting: Which did Cyrus have in mind: a reference for hazel-jit's output, a tool to use, or a different compiler for Hazel itself?

A short note on how BuckleScript, ReScript and Melange compile the same small program, beside hazel-jit's output (^ticket(698)).

sections.title: 2. hazeljs for other JavaScript developers
sections.intro: hazeljs is Hazel as a JavaScript library, on npm since 2026-11-02, and Messed Up Dress Up is the first program to use it for its scripts (a Hazlet: a JS program whose event handlers are written in Hazel). The next step is people outside the project: first, the group in Cambridge Cyrus mentioned, who simulate Petri nets with JS tools of their own.

items.title: A PR to dev: Hazel's README links to the experimental hazeljs package
items.body:
Opened 2026-11-06: #2812 (branch docs/readme-hazeljs, README only; CI running). A small PR against dev: a short section in Hazel's README on hazeljs, the experimental npm package (source: hazelgrove/hazeljs; 0.0.4 is the latest): Hazel as a JavaScript library, to analyze and run Hazel programs from Node or a web page and call the functions they define. It notes that the plan is for the package to track dev, but that it does not yet: it is built from the draft library in #2711 and #2719 (at 1ba138ef28). At the last meeting, hazeljs following dev was settled as the direction, perhaps after #2469 lands, and not urgent.

Why now: Cyrus knows people in Cambridge who simulate Petri nets with JavaScript tools of their own. Matthew would like to see whether they could move some of their JS logic into Hazel through hazeljs, to gain Hazel's types and its clarity in the middle of an edit. A link from Hazel's own README gives them a place to start.
items.meeting: Who should review it? And Cyrus's contacts in Cambridge: who they are, and whether he will introduce them.

items.title: A report for JS developers: scripting your app in Hazel, the way MUDU does
items.status: drafted: ^report(43) live, ^report(44), and the example app live at 0.0.10
items.body:
Update, 11-07: the example app is live, at 0.0.10 (matthewhammer.org/hazeljs-petri-example). Its rules on the left, each in Hazel's editor, with any error under the rule it is in; the net on the right, written in Hazel too, editable, and drawn again from its definition after every edit; a divider, and full screen. hazeljs is at 0.0.6 on npm: an object's keys in any order (the bug the example found, fixed in Hazel at 6c283c8a9f), and its listings script in the package, breaking long lines to fit each listing (hazelgrove/hazeljs#1, closed). Reports 043 and 044 use that script. The editable embed they rely on is a PR, #2814 (js-library-embed), open.

Since 2026-11-06 afternoon: ^report(43)'s example runs on its page, every Hazel listing in Hazel's own editor with go to definition between listings, and an event log as the game's; ^report(44) says how any article can have such listings; and the example is an app of its own, in a public repository, matthewhammer/hazeljs-petri-example (0.0.1; its site, in the game's style, is planned). hazeljs's README now has both apps under Examples, with links to the two reports. Building it found a bug in hazeljs: a JS object whose keys come in another order than its type's fields gets stuck when a field is a list.

Drafted 2026-11-06: ^report(43), Scripting a JavaScript App in Hazel (work in progress). It explains the pattern and the game's pieces, with links to their lines in the game's code, then six steps for another app, then a worked Petri net example (two processes and a lock; the firing rule in two Hazel modules), run in Node through hazeljs 0.0.4. Its findings: the rule ran as written; in 2,000 random steps the two processes were never both busy; a mistake in a rule is reported by module before anything runs, while the app's own JS answers; a call costs about 3.5 ms against 0.7 µs for the same handler in JS, and a build 340 to 440 ms. That is fine for each click, but not for a simulator's inner loop, which ties this item to hazel-jit (item 2).

A Hazel report on how Messed Up Dress Up uses hazeljs for its scripts, written for another JavaScript developer who wants to do the same in their own program. It builds on ^report(33) (the game's scripts), ^report(34) (a library for Hazel in JS) and ^report(39) (Hazlets so far), but speaks to someone outside the project.

What it would cover: (1) the shape: the app hands an event and a typed view of its state to a Hazel function, and acts out the command it returns; Hazel never touches the page. (2) How the game does it: each room's on_event : (Globals, Event) -> Cmd, a program of modules (Common, then one per room) built by Hazel.runProgram, errors and holes reported module by module, the game's own JS answering while the program is unfinished, and the event log. (3) The steps for your app: install, write the types, call the function per event, interpret the commands. (4) Costs and limits today: a Hazel rule answers in about 3.5 ms of a 13.7 ms lever pull, the first event after a reset waits 0.5 to 0.7 s, and the package is a 0.0.x prototype. (5) A small worked example in another domain, perhaps a Petri net's firing rule, for the readers in Cambridge.
items.meeting: Is a Petri-net example the right one for Cyrus's contacts, and what would their tools need from a Hazel rule? Is ^report(43) ready to send them as it is, or after the example is a web page (its What next, step 3)?
